claim: Intrauterine growth restriction affects up to 10% of the population.
source: Insufficient fetal substrate supply prevents the fetus from achieving its genetic growth potential and leads to intrauterine growth restriction, which affects up to 10% of the population and is associated with perinatal morbidity and mortality (Baschat et al., 2007; Baschat and Hecher, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baschat et al., 2007 and Baschat and Hecher, 2004.

claim: Intrauterine growth restriction is associated with perinatal morbidity and mortality.
source: Insufficient fetal substrate supply prevents the fetus from achieving its genetic growth potential and leads to intrauterine growth restriction, which affects up to 10% of the population and is associated with perinatal morbidity and mortality (Baschat et al., 2007; Baschat and Hecher, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baschat et al., 2007 and Baschat and Hecher, 2004.

claim: The transport capacity of the placenta is diminished in human pregnancies associated with fetal growth restriction.
source: Studies have shown that the transport capacity of the placenta is diminished in human pregnancies associated with fetal growth restriction (Glazier et al., 1997; Jansson and Powell, 2006), suggesting that placental insufficiency may be the underlying cause of a fetus failing to achieve its genetic growth potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glazier et al., 1997 and Jansson and Powell, 2006.

claim: Placental transport capacity may adapt to maintain the supply of resources appropriate for the growth potential of the fetus.
source: However, there is also evidence that placental transport capacity may adapt to maintain the supply of resources appropriate for the growth potential of the fetus (Sandovici et al., 2012; Sferruzzi-Perri and Camm, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sandovici et al., 2012 and Sferruzzi-Perri and Camm, 2016.

claim: The placental capacity to supply resources to the fetus is higher in the lightest compared to heaviest placentas, supporting babies within the normal birth weight range.
source: For instance, the placental capacity to supply resources to the fetus is higher in the lightest compared to heaviest placentas, supporting babies within the normal birth weight range (Godfrey et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Godfrey et al., 1998.

claim: Placental supply capacity is increased in newborns showing some protection to the growth-restricting effects of altitude-induced hypoxia.
source: Placental supply capacity is also increased in newborns showing some protection to the growth-restricting effects of altitude-induced hypoxia (Espinoza et al., 2001; Jackson et al., 1988; Moore et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Espinoza et al., 2001, Jackson et al., 1988, and Moore et al., 2001.

claim: The placenta can adaptively up-regulate its transport function when the fetal demand for resources exceeds the supply capacity of the placenta in mice.
source: Studies in mice have also shown that the placenta can adaptively up-regulate its transport function when the fetal demand for resources exceeds the supply capacity of the placenta, including following reduced expression of nutrient transporter or growth-regulatory genes, in small placentas within litters, and when the maternal provision of substrates is suboptimal (Coan et al., 2008; Constância et al., 2005; Dilworth et al., 2010; Higgins et al., 2016; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2011; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2013b; Vaughan et al., 2013; Wyrwoll et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to mouse studies.

claim: PI3Ks are a highly conserved family of enzymes thought to have evolved to regulate growth in relation to nutrient supply.
source: The phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are a highly conserved family of enzymes, which are thought to have evolved to regulate growth in relation to nutrient supply (Engelman et al., 2006; Kriplani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Engelman et al., 2006 and Kriplani et al., 2015.

claim: PI3Ks generate lipid second messengers to initiate signaling cascades that control cellular proliferation, metabolism, survival, polarity and membrane trafficking.
source: In response to receptor activation, they generate lipid second messengers to initiate signaling cascades, which control important physiological processes such as cellular proliferation, metabolism, survival, polarity and membrane trafficking (Vanhaesebroeck et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vanhaesebroeck et al., 2010.

claim: Class IA PI3K isoform p110α plays a key role in mediating the growth and metabolic effects of insulin and insulin-like growth factors in adult mammalian tissues.
source: In adult mammalian tissues, the ubiquitously expressed, Class IA isoform p110α plays a key role in mediating the growth and metabolic effects of insulin and insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) (Foukas et al., 2006; Knight et al., 2006; Sopasakis et al., 2010), which are major growth factors that also operate during feto-placental development (Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2017; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Foukas et al., 2006, Knight et al., 2006, and Sopasakis et al., 2010.

claim: Changes in the PI3K pathway, particularly downstream of p110α, are observed in placentas showing adaptive up-regulation of substrate supply to the fetus in pregnancies challenged with poor maternal environments and genetically-induced placental growth restriction in mice.
source: Studies in mice show that changes in the PI3K pathway, particularly downstream of p110α are observed in placentas showing adaptive up-regulation of substrate supply to the fetus in pregnancies challenged with poor maternal environments and genetically-induced placental growth restriction (Higgins et al., 2016; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2011; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Higgins et al., 2016, Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2011, and Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2013b.

claim: Homozygous p110α deficiency in mice results in embryonic death between gestation day 9.5 and 11.5.
source: Studies in mice have indicated that homozygous p110α deficiency, either by the complete loss of Pik3ca gene or by a mutation in Pik3ca which renders the p110α inactive (kinase dead mutation; p110αD933A/D933A; α/α), results in embryonic death between gestation day 9.5 and 11.5 (Bi et al., 1999; Foukas et al., 2006; Graupera et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bi et al., 1999, Foukas et al., 2006, and Graupera et al., 2008.

claim: Mice carrying one copy of the kinase-dead p110α mutation (p110αD933A/+; α/+) are viable but weigh 10–15% less than their wildtype littermates in late gestation.
source: When p110α activity is reduced by half, in mice carrying one copy of the kinase-dead mutation (p110αD933A/+; α/+), fetuses are viable, but weigh 10–15% less than their wildtype littermates in late gestation (Foukas et al., 2006; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Foukas et al., 2006 and Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016.

claim: Placental weight is reduced in association with defects in the development of the labyrinthine transport region in α/+ mutants.
source: Placental weight is also reduced in association with defects in the development of the labyrinthine transport region in α/+mutants (Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016.

claim: The capacity of the placenta to transfer maternal glucose and amino acid (via System A) to the fetus per unit surface area is increased in α/+ mutants near term.
source: However, the capacity of the placenta to transfer maternal glucose and amino acid (via System A) to the fetus per unit surface area is increased in α/+mutants near term (Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016.

claim: PI3K p110α is highly expressed in the placental transport labyrinthine zone and the endocrine junctional zone of the mouse placenta.
source: We found PI3K p110α was highly expressed in the placental transport labyrinthine zone and the endocrine junctional zone of the mouse placenta (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cyp19Cre targets expression in the trophoblast lineages of the placenta but not fetus, labyrinthine fetal capillaries or mesenchyme in the chorion.
source: These Cre lines are active in opposite compartments of the conceptus; for Het-P the Cyp19Cre targets expression in the trophoblast lineages of the placenta but not fetus, labyrinthine fetal capillaries or mesenchyme in the chorion (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: Meox2Cre deletes p110α expression in the fetus and placental labyrinthine fetal capillaries and chorionic mesenchyme but not trophoblast.
source: In contrast, in Het-F the Meox2Cre deletes p110α expression in the fetus and placental labyrinthine fetal capillaries and chorionic mesenchyme but not trophoblast (Figure 1B and C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: There is no effect of heterozygous deficiency of p110α in the trophoblast on fetal or placental weight in Het-P mutants compared to wild-type littermates on day 19 of pregnancy.
source: We found that compared to their wild-type (WT) littermates, there was no effect of heterozygous deficiency of p110α in the trophoblast on fetal or placental weight in Het-P mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fetal and placental weights are 10–15% lower for Het-F and Het-U conceptuses compared to wild-type littermates on day 19 of pregnancy.
source: However, fetal and placental weights were 10–15% lower for Het-F and Het-U conceptuses (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: p110α in the embryo is important for determining the size of the placenta.
source: The findings in Het-F and Het-U mutants are consistent with the proliferation defects observed in embryos with a deficiency in p110α (Bi et al., 1999; Foukas et al., 2006) and reveal for the first time that p110α in the embryo is important for determining the size of the placenta.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Het-F and Het-U mutants and citations to Bi et al., 1999 and Foukas et al., 2006.

claim: In the labyrinthine region of Het-P conceptuses, the volume of maternal blood spaces, fetal capillaries and surface area are reduced though trophoblast is increased compared to wild-type controls.
source: In the labyrinthine region of Het-P conceptuses, the volume of maternal blood spaces, fetal capillaries and surface area were reduced though trophoblast increased compared to their WT controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Het-F conceptuses, the labyrinthine zone, fetal capillaries and trophoblast volume are decreased versus wild-type littermates.
source: In Het-F conceptuses, the labyrinthine zone, fetal capillaries and trophoblast volume were decreased versus WT littermates (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Het-U conceptuses, the volume of the labyrinthine zone, fetal capillaries and trophoblast are reduced, surface area is decreased and barrier to diffusion is greater, relative to wild-type littermates.
source: In the ubiquitous p110α heterozygote (Het-U), the volume of the labyrinthine zone, fetal capillaries and trophoblast were reduced, surface area decreased and barrier to diffusion was greater, relative to WT littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The volume of the endocrine junctional zone in Het-P, Het-F or Het-U placentas is not significantly altered when compared to the respective wild-type controls.
source: The volume of the endocrine junctional zone in Het-P, Het-F or Het-U placentas was not significantly altered when compared to the respective WT controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Het-P and Het-U placentas transfer more MeG and MeAIB per unit surface area compared to their respective wild-type littermates.
source: We found that in compensation for the impaired labyrinthine development, Het-P and Het-U placentas transferred more MeG and MeAIB and Het-F more MeAIB per unit surface area compared to their respective WT littermates (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Het-F placentas transfer more MeAIB per unit surface area compared to wild-type littermates.
source: We found that in compensation for the impaired labyrinthine development, Het-P and Het-U placentas transferred more MeG and MeAIB and Het-F more MeAIB per unit surface area compared to their respective WT littermates (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Mutant fetuses (Het-P, Het-F, Het-U) receive either normal or increased amounts of solutes for their size.
source: In agreement with these findings, mutant fetuses received either normal (MeG in all mutants and MeAIB in Het-P and Het-F) or increased amount of solutes (MeAIB in Het-U) for their size (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: The total fetal accumulation of MeG and MeAIB solutes is the same in the mutant and wild-type fetuses.
source: Moreover, the total fetal accumulation of these solutes was the same in the mutant and WT fetuses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deleting the remaining p110α from the fetal lineages (Hom-F) is lethal between days 11 and 12 of pregnancy.
source: We found that deleting the remaining p110α from the fetal lineages was lethal between days 11 and 12 of pregnancy (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Viable Hom-P fetuses are found in late gestation.
source: In contrast to the lethality of Hom-F embryos, we found viable Hom-P fetuses in late gestation (Figure 1C and Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Table 1—source data 1.

claim: The timing of Hom-F lethality is identical to mutants with constitutive homozygous deficiency of p110α (α/α).
source: The timing of Hom-F lethality was identical to mutants with constitutive homozygous deficiency of p110α (α/α; Foukas et al., 2006) and is consistent with the role of p110α in early murine embryonic development (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foukas et al., 2006.

claim: p110α in the fetal, but not the trophoblast compartment of the conceptus, is obligatory for prenatal development.
source: Taken together, these findings highlight that p110α in the fetal, but not the trophoblast compartment of the conceptus, is obligatory for prenatal development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lethality of Hom-F but viability of Hom-P mutants.

claim: Fetal growth is restricted by a further 8% in Hom-P conceptuses compared to Het-U littermates on day 19 of pregnancy.
source: When comparing the growth of the Hom-P conceptuses to the control Het-U littermates, we found that fetal growth was restricted by a further 8% on day 19 of pregnancy (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: There is no difference in placental weight and labyrinthine morphology in Hom-P versus Het-U on day 19 of pregnancy.
source: However, despite the reduction in fetal growth, there was no difference in placental weight and labyrinthine morphology in Hom-P versus Het-U (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Hom-P placentas transfer 30% less amino acid (MeAIB) for the surface area available than Het-U littermates.
source: We found that Hom-P placentas transferred 30% less amino acid (MeAIB) for the surface area available than Het-U littermates (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hom-P fetuses receive less MeAIB solute for their size, as well as overall.
source: Furthermore, Hom-P fetuses received less MeAIB solute for their size, as well as overall (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Placental glucose transfer capacity is not affected by a lack of placental p110α; transfer of MeG by the Hom-P placenta is equal to Het-U.
source: Placental glucose transfer capacity however, was not affected by a lack of placental p110α; transfer of MeG by the Hom-P placenta was equal to Het-U (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 97 differentially expressed genes were identified between Hom-P and Het-U placentas at day 19 of pregnancy, with 61 up-regulated and 36 down-regulated in Hom-P versus Het-U placenta.
source: We identified 97 differentially expressed genes, with 61 up- and 36 down-regulated in Hom-P versus Het-U placenta (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: The FPKM for the floxed exons 18–19 of Pik3ca is diminished for Hom-P versus Het-U.
source: As expected, the FPKM (fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads) for the floxed exons, 18–19 of Pik3ca (Graupera et al., 2008) was diminished for Hom-P versus Het-U (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genes down-regulated in Hom-P compared with Het-U placentas have been implicated in cytolysis and cell death, proteolysis, regulation of immune effector processes.
source: Using DAVID functional annotation followed by REViGO filtering we found that genes that were down-regulated in Hom-P compared with Het-U placentas have been implicated in cytolysis and cell death, proteolysis, regulation of immune effector processes, whilst those that were up-regulated have proposed roles in cellular hormone metabolic processes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes up-regulated in Hom-P compared with Het-U placentas have proposed roles in cellular hormone metabolic processes.
source: Using DAVID functional annotation followed by REViGO filtering we found that genes that were down-regulated in Hom-P compared with Het-U placentas have been implicated in cytolysis and cell death, proteolysis, regulation of immune effector processes, whilst those that were up-regulated have proposed roles in cellular hormone metabolic processes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no significant difference in uterine natural killer cell abundance between Hom-P and Het-U placentas.
source: However, we found no significant difference in uterine natural killer cell abundance between Hom-P and Het-U placentas (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: There are increased levels of apoptosis in the junctional zone of the Hom-P relative to the Het-U placenta.
source: Moreover, paradoxically, we found increased levels of apoptosis in the junctional zone of the Hom-P relative to the Het-U placenta (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Expression of the main glucose and System A amino acid transporters (Slc2a, Slc38a) and their proposed regulators (Mtor, Tbc1d4) is not different between Hom-P and Het-U placentas.
source: Inspecting the list of genes from the RNA-seq dataset revealed that expression of the main glucose and System A amino acid transporters (Slc2a, Slc38a) and their proposed regulators (Mtor, Tbc1d4) (Mîinea et al., 2005; Rosario et al., 2013) was not different between Hom-P and Het-U placentas.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Genes involved in water and oxygen transport (eg. Aqp1, Aqp5, Hba-a2) are altered between Hom-P and Het-U placentas.
source: However, genes involved in water and oxygen transport (eg. Aqp1, Aqp5, Hba-a2) were altered (Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that other transport capabilities of the placenta may be altered and contribute to the greater fetal growth restriction observed in the Hom-P versus Het-U.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Significant enrichment of binding sites for four transcription factors (STAT1, ARNT2, HMGA1 and MITF) is found at the promoters of genes differentially expressed between Hom-P and Het-U placenta.
source: We next identified significant enrichment of binding sites for four transcription factors (STAT1, ARNT2, HMGA1 and MITF) at the promoters of genes differentially expressed between Hom-P and Het-U placenta (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: The mRNA expression of the transcription factors STAT1, ARNT2, HMGA1 and MITF is not altered in the Hom-P versus Het-U placenta.
source: The mRNA expression of the transcription factors were not altered in the Hom-P versus Het-U placenta (Figure 6—source data 1), although previous work has shown that their activity is modified by PI3K signaling (Mounayar et al., 2015; Sheu et al., 2017; Terragni et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2018) and/or implicated in the development of pregnancy complications related to placental dysfunction (Than et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: 46 of the differentially expressed genes between Hom-P and Het-U placentas are expressed in both trophoblast and embryonic stem cells.
source: We found that 46 of DEGs were expressed in both cell types, and of these, 26 were highly enriched in the TS compared to the ES cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: 26 of the differentially expressed genes between Hom-P and Het-U placentas are highly enriched in trophoblast stem cells compared to embryonic stem cells.
source: We found that 46 of DEGs were expressed in both cell types, and of these, 26 were highly enriched in the TS compared to the ES cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of p110α significantly reduces the expression of B2m in mutant trophoblast stem cells.
source: Loss of p110α significantly reduced the expression of B2m in mutant TS cells (Figure 7D), similar to findings in vivo from the Hom-P versus Het-U placenta (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: p110α deficiency significantly increases the expression of Cited2, Pdlim3, Creb3l1, Mgst1, Aldh1a3 in embryonic stem cells.
source: For instance, p110α deficiency significantly increased the expression of Cited2, Pdlim3, Creb3l1, Mgst1, Aldh1a3 in the ES cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pathways downstream of p110α differentially affect the expression of genes in the trophoblast and fetal cell lineages of the conceptus.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that pathways downstream of p110α differentially affect the expression of genes in the trophoblast and fetal cell lineages of the conceptus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns observed in trophoblast stem cells versus embryonic stem cells with p110α deficiency.

claim: p110α in the fetal, but not the trophoblast compartment of the conceptus determines placental size in late mouse pregnancy.
source: The data presented here indicate that p110α in the fetal, but not the trophoblast compartment of the conceptus determines placental size in late mouse pregnancy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Het-F but not Het-P showed reduced placental weight.

claim: Reduced fetal capillary formation in the labyrinthine zone of the Het-F could underlie the reduced placental weight and labyrinthine zone observed.
source: Reduced fetal capillary formation in the labyrinthine zone of the Het-F could therefore underlie the reduced placental weight and labyrinthine zone observed and data are consistent with previous work showing defective angiogenesis and vascular development in the fetus and placenta in response to p110α loss (Graupera et al., 2008; Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Graupera et al., 2008 and Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2016.

claim: Epiblast-derived and trophoblast p110α have non-overlapping contributions in regulating the development of the placental exchange region.
source: Our stereological analyses of the Het-F, Het-P and Het-U placentas demonstrated that epiblast-derived and trophoblast p110α have non-overlapping contributions in regulating the development of the placental exchange region.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the distinct morphological phenotypes observed in Het-F versus Het-P placentas.

claim: p110α in the epiblast-derived compartment determines the size of the placental labyrinthine zone and its trophoblast constituent.
source: In particular, p110α in the epiblast-derived compartment determined the size of the placental labyrinthine zone and its trophoblast constituent, whereas p110α in the trophoblast was important for expanding the surface area for maternal-fetal exchange.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stereological analysis of Het-F placentas.

claim: p110α in the trophoblast is important for expanding the surface area for maternal-fetal exchange.
source: In particular, p110α in the epiblast-derived compartment determined the size of the placental labyrinthine zone and its trophoblast constituent, whereas p110α in the trophoblast was important for expanding the surface area for maternal-fetal exchange.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stereological analysis of Het-P placentas.

claim: p110α in both the trophoblast and epiblast-derived lineages contributes to the formation of the capillary network and the thinness of the diffusion barrier in the placental exchange region.
source: Moreover, p110α in both the trophoblast and epiblast-derived lineages contributed to the formation of the capillary network and the thinness of the diffusion barrier in the placental exchange region.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stereological analysis of Het-F, Het-P, and Het-U placentas.

claim: There is paracrine communication between cellular compartments in the placental labyrinthine zone, which occurs via p110α signaling.
source: As fetal capillary volume was affected by a deficiency of p110α signaling in the trophoblast and trophoblast volume was altered by a deficiency in fetal p110α, our data suggest that there is a paracrine communication between cellular compartments in the placental labyrinthine zone, which occurs via p110α signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that p110α deficiency in one compartment affects the other compartment.

claim: Adaptive up-regulation of placental amino acid transport depends on the expression of p110α in the trophoblast.
source: We found that in conceptuses with p110α deficiency, this adaptive up-regulation of placental amino acid transport depended on the expression of p110α in the trophoblast; System A-mediated amino acid transport was significantly lower for the Hom-P compared to the adapted Het-U placenta.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing reduced amino acid transport in Hom-P versus Het-U.

claim: The inability of the Hom-P placenta to up-regulate System A amino acid transport may explain, at least partly, the further reduction in fetal weight, when compared to Het-U.
source: This inability of the Hom-P placenta to up-regulate System A amino acid transport, may explain, at least partly, the further reduction in fetal weight, when compared to Het-U.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the correlation between reduced amino acid transport and reduced fetal weight.

claim: Demand signals of the compromised feto-placental unit, such as IGF2, operate via p110α in the trophoblast to adapt amino acid supply to the fetus for growth.
source: Our data therefore imply that demand signals of the compromised feto-placental unit, such as IGF2, operate via p110α in the trophoblast to adapt amino acid supply to the fetus for growth.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the data on adaptive transport and previous work on IGF2.

claim: Loss of p110α may alter glucose and amino acid transport to the fetus by the placenta via post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: In other cell types, p110α alters the activity of glucose and sodium transporters on the plasma membrane (Frevert and Kahn, 1997; Katagiri et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2008). Loss of p110α may therefore, alter glucose and amino acid transport to the fetus by the placenta via post-transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to studies in other cell types.

claim: Dysregulated expression of both up and down-stream components of the PI3K pathway in the placenta are associated with abnormal fetal growth and poor pregnancy outcome in humans.
source: Nevertheless our findings are important in the context of human pregnancy, as dysregulated expression of both up and down-stream components of the PI3K pathway in the placenta are associated with abnormal fetal growth and poor pregnancy outcome (reviewed in Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Sferruzzi-Perri et al., 2017.
